name: 1 Thessalonians
description: Shared work · remembered care · waiting · resurrection hope · alert conduct

1.text: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, to the assembly of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
We always give thanks to God for all of you, mentioning you in our prayers,
remembering without ceasing your work of faith and labor of love and perseverance of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ, before our God and Father.
We know, brothers loved by God, that you are chosen,
and that our Good News came to you not in word only, but also in power, and in the Holy Spirit and with much assurance. You know what kind of men we showed ourselves to be among you for your sake.
You became imitators of us and of the Lord, having received the word in much affliction, with joy of the Holy Spirit,
so that you became an example to all who believe in Macedonia and in Achaia.
For from you the word of the Lord has been declared, not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but also in every place your faith toward God has gone out, so that we need not say anything.
For they themselves report concerning us what kind of a reception we had from you, and how you turned to God from idols to serve a living and true God,
and to wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead: Jesus, who delivers us from the wrath to come.

2.text: For you yourselves know, brothers, our visit to you wasn’t in vain,
but having suffered before and been shamefully treated, as you know, at Philippi, we grew bold in our God to tell you the Good News of God in much conflict.
For our exhortation is not of error, nor of uncleanness, nor in deception.
But even as we have been approved by God to be entrusted with the Good News, so we speak—not as pleasing men, but God, who tests our hearts.
For neither were we at any time found using words of flattery, as you know, nor a cloak of covetousness (God is witness),
nor seeking glory from men (neither from you nor from others), when we might have claimed authority as apostles of Christ.
But we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother cherishes her own children.
Even so, affectionately longing for you, we were well pleased to impart to you not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us.
For you remember, brothers, our labor and travail; for working night and day, that we might not burden any of you, we preached to you the Good News of God.
You are witnesses with God how holy, righteously, and blamelessly we behaved ourselves toward you who believe.
As you know, we exhorted, comforted, and implored every one of you, as a father does his own children,
to the end that you should walk worthily of God, who calls you into his own Kingdom and glory.

For this cause we also thank God without ceasing that when you received from us the word of the message of God, you accepted it not as the word of men, but as it is in truth, God’s word, which also works in you who believe.
For you, brothers, became imitators of the assemblies of God which are in Judea in Christ Jesus; for you also suffered the same things from your own countrymen, even as they did from the Jews
who killed both the Lord Jesus and their own prophets, and drove us out, and don’t please God, and are contrary to all men,
forbidding us to speak to the Gentiles that they may be saved, to fill up their sins always. But wrath has come on them to the uttermost.
But we, brothers, being bereaved of you for a short season in presence, not in heart, tried even harder to see your face with great desire,
because we wanted to come to you—indeed, I, Paul, once and again—but Satan hindered us.
For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of rejoicing? Isn’t it even you, before our Lord Jesus at his coming?
For you are our glory and our joy.

3.text: Therefore when we couldn’t stand it any longer, we thought it good to be left behind at Athens alone,
and sent Timothy, our brother and God’s servant in the Good News of Christ, to establish you and to comfort you concerning your faith,
that no one would be moved by these afflictions. For you know that we are appointed to this task.
For most certainly, when we were with you, we told you beforehand that we are to suffer affliction, even as it happened, and you know.
For this cause I also, when I couldn’t stand it any longer, sent that I might know your faith, for fear that by any means the tempter had tempted you, and our labor would have been in vain.
But Timothy has just now come to us from you, and brought us glad news of your faith and love, and that you have good memories of us always, longing to see us, even as we also long to see you.
For this cause, brothers, we were comforted over you in all our distress and affliction through your faith.
For now we live, if you stand fast in the Lord.
For what thanksgiving can we give again to God for you, for all the joy with which we rejoice for your sakes before our God,
night and day praying exceedingly that we may see your face and may perfect that which is lacking in your faith?
Now may our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus Christ, direct our way to you.
May the Lord make you to increase and abound in love toward one another and toward all men, even as we also do toward you,
to the end he may establish your hearts blameless in holiness before our God and Father at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints.

4.text: Finally then, brothers, we beg and exhort you in the Lord Jesus, that as you received from us how you ought to walk and to please God, that you abound more and more.
For you know what instructions we gave you through the Lord Jesus.
For this is the will of God: your sanctification, that you abstain from sexual immorality,
that each one of you know how to control his own body in sanctification and honor,
not in the passion of lust, even as the Gentiles who don’t know God,
that no one should take advantage of and wrong a brother or sister in this matter; because the Lord is an avenger in all these things, as also we forewarned you and testified.
For God called us not for uncleanness, but in sanctification.
Therefore he who rejects this doesn’t reject man, but God, who has also given his Holy Spirit to you.
But concerning brotherly love, you have no need that one write to you. For you yourselves are taught by God to love one another,
for indeed you do it toward all the brothers who are in all Macedonia. But we exhort you, brothers, that you abound more and more;
and that you make it your ambition to lead a quiet life, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, even as we instructed you,
that you may walk properly toward those who are outside, and may have need of nothing.
But we don’t want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who have fallen asleep, so that you don’t grieve like the rest, who have no hope.
For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep in Jesus.
For this we tell you by the word of the Lord, that we who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will in no way precede those who have fallen asleep.
For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel and with God’s trumpet. The dead in Christ will rise first,
then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air. So we will be with the Lord forever.
Therefore comfort one another with these words.

5.text: But concerning the times and the seasons, brothers, you have no need that anything be written to you.
For you yourselves know well that the day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night.
For when they are saying, “Peace and safety,” then sudden destruction will come on them, like birth pains on a pregnant woman. Then they will in no way escape.
But you, brothers, aren’t in darkness, that the day should overtake you like a thief.
You are all children of light and children of the day. We don’t belong to the night, nor to darkness,
so then let’s not sleep, as the rest do, but let’s watch and be sober.
For those who sleep, sleep in the night; and those who are drunk are drunk in the night.
But since we belong to the day, let’s be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet, the hope of salvation.
For God didn’t appoint us to wrath, but to the obtaining of salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ,
who died for us, that, whether we wake or sleep, we should live together with him.
Therefore exhort one another, and build each other up, even as you also do.
But we beg you, brothers, to know those who labor among you, and are over you in the Lord and admonish you,
and to respect and honor them in love for their work’s sake. Be at peace among yourselves.
We exhort you, brothers: Admonish the disorderly; encourage the faint-hearted; support the weak; be patient toward all.
See that no one returns evil for evil to anyone, but always follow after that which is good for one another and for all.
Always rejoice.
Pray without ceasing.
In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you.
Don’t quench the Spirit.
Don’t despise prophecies.
Test all things, and hold firmly that which is good.
Abstain from every form of evil.
May the God of peace himself sanctify you completely. May your whole spirit, soul, and body be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.
He who calls you is faithful, who will also do it.
Brothers, pray for us.
Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss.
I solemnly command you by the Lord that this letter be read to all the holy brothers.
The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Amen.

chapters.title: The hearers' received faith becomes an example during continued suffering
chapters.summary: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy write to the assembly of the Thessalonians. They thank God for the readers’ faith, love, and enduring hope. The good news came to them in power and in the Holy Spirit. They received the word in much affliction with joy. They became an example to believers in Macedonia and Achaia. People everywhere tell how they turned from idols to serve the living God. They wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised.
chapters.meaning: Verse 5 says the readers saw what kind of men the writers were. Verse 6 says the readers then became imitators of them and of the Lord. The likeness is specific. They received the word in much affliction. They also received it with joy from the Holy Spirit. Trouble and joy together is the pattern they copied. Verse 7 shows it passing on: they became an example to other believers.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson teaches sincere sharing through a faithful personal example. How does receiving the message amid suffering become an example to others?

chapters.historicalNote: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy open together before giving thanks for the hearers' changed life. Faith, love, and hope appear through work and endurance rather than private feeling alone. The hearers first imitate their teachers and the Lord while receiving the message amid suffering. They then become examples whose changed service carries news beyond their own group. Turning from idols describes a new direction rather than a claim that every difficulty ended. Waiting for the risen Son places their present endurance within the future hope named here.

chapters.title: Remembered care supports trust while painful separation remains unresolved
chapters.summary: Paul recalls that they came to Thessalonica after being mistreated at Philippi. They did not use flattery or seek glory or money. They were gentle, like a nursing mother with her children. They worked night and day so as not to burden anyone. They urged each one as a father does. The readers accepted the message as God’s word and suffered from their own countrymen. Paul speaks sharply of those in Judea who opposed the assemblies there. He wanted to return, but Satan hindered him, and the readers are his joy.
chapters.meaning: Verses 3–6 deny wrong motives: deceit, flattery, greed, and a search for glory. Verse 7 gives the opposite picture: a nursing mother. Verse 8 says what that care amounted to. They gave the good news, and they gave their own souls. The reason is affection: the readers had become very dear to them. Verse 9 offers proof the readers can remember: labor night and day.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson teaches sharing the gospel with sincerity and love. Why does Paul ask the hearers to remember the teachers' own conduct?

chapters.historicalNote: Paul appeals to the hearers' memories of work, shared life, and refusal of greedy demands. David Carr reads these appeals as a defense of the team's trustworthiness. Mother and father images join tender care with encouragement toward a worthy life. The comparison with Judean assemblies then places the hearers' suffering beside another group's suffering. The harsh accusations concern this letter's conflict rather than every Jewish person across time. The final account of blocked visits shows that affection has not yet overcome separation.

chapters.title: Timothy's report turns fear about separation into comfort and renewed prayer
chapters.summary: Paul could not bear the separation and sent Timothy from Athens. Timothy was to strengthen them so that no one would be shaken by afflictions. Paul had warned them that suffering would come. He feared the tempter had tempted them and the work was wasted. Timothy has now returned with good news of their faith and love. Paul says he lives if they stand firm in the Lord. He prays night and day to see them and supply what their faith lacks. He prays that their love will increase.
chapters.meaning: Verse 5 states Paul’s fear: the tempter may have undone the work. He sent Timothy because he could bear it no longer. Verse 6 reports the answer, and it has three parts. Their faith holds, their love holds, and they remember the writers kindly. The third part matters to a man torn away from them (2:17). They long to see him as he longs to see them. Verse 7 says this comforted him in his own distress.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson connects increased love with growing holiness. How does Timothy's report give comfort to the teachers as well as the hearers?

chapters.historicalNote: The previous account of blocked visits explains why sending Timothy matters to the speaker. Leaving Athens without him allows concern for the hearers to take priority over immediate companionship. The feared failure concerns their response to suffering rather than a lack of contact alone. Timothy's report of faith and love gives the teachers comfort in their own distress. Their wish to supply what is lacking does not cancel recognition of received good news. The closing prayer asks that increased love prepare their hearts for the Lord's coming.

chapters.title: Careful conduct and hope for the dead answer different forms of harm and fear
chapters.summary: Paul urges them to live so as to please God, more and more. God’s will is their holiness, and they are to abstain from sexual immorality. No one should wrong a brother in this matter. They already love one another and should do so more. They should live quietly, mind their own business, and work with their hands. Paul then writes about those who have fallen asleep. The dead in Christ will rise first, when the Lord descends with a shout. Then the living will be caught up to be with the Lord always.
chapters.meaning: Verse 13 gives the purpose of the passage. Paul does not want them to grieve like those who have no hope. The worry seems to be that the dead will miss the Lord’s coming. Verse 15 answers it: the living will not go ahead of the dead. Verse 16 puts the dead in Christ first. Verse 17 ends with all of them together with the Lord. Verse 18 tells them to use these words to comfort each other.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson teaches gradual growth in holiness and work that supports others. Why does the account of the dead end with shared comfort?

chapters.historicalNote: The first commands join bodily conduct with a refusal to take advantage of another person. Brotherly love then requires continued growth alongside quiet work and care toward outsiders. The turn to those who sleep names death as the next concern requiring instruction. The appeal permits grief but distinguishes grief without hope from grief shaped by resurrection. Living believers receive no earlier place than those who died before the Lord's coming. The account ends with shared comfort rather than a date or permission to abandon work.

chapters.title: An unknown day calls for alert care rather than a calculated schedule
chapters.summary: Paul says they need no letter about times and seasons. The day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night. They are children of light and should stay awake and sober. They wear faith and love as a breastplate and hope as a helmet. They should respect those who labor among them and lead them. Paul gives short commands: rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in everything. They should not quench the Spirit, and they should test all things. He asks that the letter be read to all the brothers.
chapters.meaning: Verses 12–13 speak of those who lead. Verse 14 then gives a task to the “brothers,” the whole group. It names three kinds of people and three different responses. The disorderly are admonished, the faint-hearted encouraged, and the weak supported. One response covers everyone: patience. Verse 15 adds the limit: no one may repay evil for evil.

lds.text: How do different needs require different kinds of care?

chapters.historicalNote: The thief and birth images show why the day cannot depend on confident human prediction. Being children of light therefore requires alert conduct rather than knowledge of a hidden date. Faith, love, and hope become protective equipment within that task of waiting together. The appeal assigns different care to disorderly, discouraged, and weak members instead of one response. Testing what is heard joins openness to the Spirit rather than replacing it with rejection. Prayer for the teachers and public reading keep the ending within the group's shared life.

people.name: Paul
people.role: Writer who sent Timothy and longs to see the Thessalonians
people.relations: He writes with Silvanus and Timothy. He sent Timothy to the Thessalonians.
people.meaning: Paul recalls how he and his team worked among the Thessalonians. He says Satan hindered his visits. He sent Timothy to learn about their faith. Timothy’s good news comforts Paul. Paul asks that the letter be read to all the brothers.
people.life: Birth and death years are not securely known.

people.name: Silvanus
people.role: Co-sender named with Paul and Timothy
people.relations: The letter names him second, between Paul and Timothy.
people.meaning: The letter names Silvanus in the opening line with Paul and Timothy. The letter says “we” after that. It says nothing else about him by name.
people.life: Birth and death years are not securely known.

people.name: Timothy
people.role: Co-sender whom Paul sent to the Thessalonians
people.relations: He is named with Paul and Silvanus. Paul calls him our brother and God’s servant.
people.meaning: Paul sends Timothy to establish and comfort the Thessalonians in their faith. Timothy comes back with glad news of their faith and love. The news comforts Paul in his distress and affliction.
people.life: Birth and death years are not securely known.

people.name: Jesus Christ
people.role: Lord who rose from the dead and will come
people.relations: Paul calls him the Lord Jesus Christ and God’s Son. He says God raised him from the dead.
people.meaning: Paul says the Thessalonians wait for God’s Son from heaven. Paul says Jesus died and rose again. He says the dead in Christ will rise first. He tells the readers to comfort one another with these words.
people.life: Birth and death years are not securely known.
